summary: Specifies a small modification to the ARP mechanism, without changing the packet format, that lets a node announce it is leaving the network so other nodes can update their ARP tables. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: When you leave a room, you tell people so they take your name off the seating chart.

questions: how to remove an arp entry when a node leaves
how to remove an arp cache entry
subtitle: A way for a node, or a proxy ARP server, to tell the LAN that an address mapping is no longer valid.

tldr.problem: ARP caches only age out old entries with timers, so after a dial-in host disconnects and reconnects through a different server, other hosts keep sending packets to the old one.
tldr.mechanism: The server broadcasts an UNARP, an unsolicited ARP Reply with a hardware address length of 0, and receivers delete the ARP cache entry for the named IP address.
tldr.outcome: The packet format is not changed, but the abbreviated packet means nodes without UNARP support should reject it.

today: RFC 1868 is an Experimental protocol, not an Internet standard, and the unit metadata shows no later RFC replacing it.

sections.title: ARP and Proxy ARP
sections.content:
The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) finds a node's hardware address from its protocol address. ARP says nodes should not periodically advertise their existence, because that would create network traffic and table maintenance and not every node needs to talk to every other. So a node does not announce its departure either, and implementations rely on timers to age away old entries.

A later use of ARP is Proxy ARP, where a server answers an ARP Request on behalf of a dial-in host. This lets dial-in hosts share the subnet address of the LAN and so avoids using up a large amount of IP address space.
sections.eli5: Computers normally do not announce when they arrive or leave. They just forget old entries after a while.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
The memo's example has Host A on a LAN with two communication servers, CS1 and CS2, whose modems share a rotary. A remote host dials into CS1. Host A sends an ARP Request, CS1 replies with its own hardware address, and traffic flows through CS1.

Then the remote host disconnects and reconnects through CS2 before Host A ages out its ARP cache entry. Host A keeps sending packets to CS1, because it cannot know the entry is invalid.
sections.eli5: Imagine a friend moves to a different desk, but you still send notes to the old desk because nobody told you.

sections.title: The UNARP Packet
sections.content:
When a server disconnects from a remote host for which it sent a Proxy ARP reply, it broadcasts an UNARP: an unsolicited ARP Reply with the field values shown below. The note says this is a 16-byte packet, not including the MAC header.

A node receiving an UNARP deletes the ARP cache entry for that IP address. A server need not remember whether it sent a Proxy ARP reply and may always send an UNARP when a remote host disconnects. A host that detaches gracefully may send an UNARP for itself, which helps if it might return with a different hardware address.
sections.eli5: It is a short shout to the whole room: forget this address, I am not here any more.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility
sections.content:
Nodes with and without UNARP support will coexist for a time. To stop nodes without support from adding bogus cache entries with hardware addresses of zero, UNARP sets the hardware address length to zero, which such nodes should reject. As a result the source and target hardware address fields do not exist in the packet.

Implementors are advised to include a configuration switch to disable UNARP in case some vendor's ARP implementation takes offense at the abbreviated packet. The memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: The message is written so that older computers see it looks wrong and ignore it instead of being confused.

items.label: Hardware Address Length
items.desc: Makes nodes without UNARP support reject the packet.

items.label: Source Hardware Address
items.desc: Absent because the hardware address length is zero.

items.label: Source Protocol Address
items.desc: The address to remove from ARP caches.

items.label: Target Hardware Address
items.desc: Absent because the hardware address length is zero.

references.text: Plummer, D., "An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol", STD 37, RFC 826, MIT, November 1982.
